hmmt-feb-2013-team-01.title: Square the ratio
hmmt-feb-2013-team-01.body:
Let $t=\frac{ab}{a^2+b^2}=\frac14$ and $u=\frac{a^2-b^2}{a^2+b^2}$. Then $u^2+4t^2=\frac{(a^2-b^2)^2+4a^2b^2}{(a^2+b^2)^2}=1$, so $u^2=1-4\cdot\frac1{16}=\frac34$ and $|u|=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.

This value occurs: take $a=1$ and solve $b^2-4b+1=0$, so $b=2\pm\sqrt3$ (real), giving $\frac{|1-b^2|}{1+b^2}=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt3}2$**

hmmt-feb-2013-team-02.title: Lower bound and construction
hmmt-feb-2013-team-02.body:
Look at the moment just before the last table is occupied.

*Case 1: the counter still has an empty seat.* Then no group of one has taken a table so far, and the group taking the last table is also not a single (it would have gone to the counter). So each of the three tables holds a group of at least $2$ people and contributes at least $1+2=3$ to $M+N$. At the end the counter is full with $5$ people, who need at least $2$ groups (a group has at most $4$ people), contributing at least $5+2=7$. Total $\ge 3\cdot3+7=16$.

*Case 2: the counter is already full.* Everyone at the counter arrived as a single (a bigger group would have chosen a free table, and one is still free), contributing $5+5=10$. Each table holds at least one group of at least one person, contributing at least $2$. Total $\ge10+3\cdot2=16$.

Equality: eight groups of one person, who first fill the counter and then the three tables: $M=N=8$, $M+N=16$.

**Answer: 16**

hmmt-feb-2013-team-03.title: Show $CA=CB$, then $EB=EC$
hmmt-feb-2013-team-03.body:
$OA=OC$ gives $\angle OCA=\angle OAC$. In circle $AOC$, $\angle OCA=\angle OFA$ (same arc $OA$). By tangency of $BC$ to this circle at $C$, $\angle OAC=\angle OCB$. Since $OB=OC$, $\angle OCB=\angle OBC$. So $\angle OCA=\angle OCB$: $CO$ bisects $\angle ACB$.

The bisector of $\angle ACB$ meets the circumcircle of $ABC$ again at the midpoint $M$ of arc $AB$, and $M$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$; so does $O$. The bisector passes through $O\ne M$ and through $M$, so it is the line $OM$, the perpendicular bisector of $AB$. Then $C$ lies on it, so $CA=CB=7$.

Next, $\angle OBC=\angle OCB=\angle OAC=\angle OFA=\angle OFB$, hence $\triangle EOB\sim\triangle EBF$ and $EB^2=EO\cdot EF$. Power of the point $E$ with respect to circle $AOC$ (tangent at $C$): $EC^2=EO\cdot EF$. So $EB=EC$ and $BE=\frac12BC=\frac72$.

**Answer: $\frac72$**

hmmt-feb-2013-team-04.title: Fractional parts and a cyclic split
hmmt-feb-2013-team-04.body:
Write $\lfloor a_i+a_j\rfloor=(a_i+a_j)-\{a_i+a_j\}$. Each $a_i$ appears in $4$ pairs, so $\sum(a_i+a_j)=4\cdot20=80$, and we must maximize $\sum_{i<j}\{a_i+a_j\}$.

Split the $10$ pairs into two $5$-cycles (indices mod $5$): $\sum_i\{a_i+a_{i+1}\}$ and $\sum_i\{a_i+a_{i+2}\}$. In each cycle every $a_i$ appears twice, so the sum of the fractional parts is congruent to $2\cdot20=40\equiv0\pmod1$: it is an integer. Each is less than $5$, so each is at most $4$. Hence $\sum\{a_i+a_j\}\le8$ and the original sum is at least $80-8=72$.

Equality: $a_1=a_2=a_3=a_4=0.4$, $a_5=18.4$. The $6$ pair sums among the first four are $0.8$ (floor $0$) and the $4$ pairs with $a_5$ give $18.8$ (floor $18$): total $72$.

**Answer: 72**

hmmt-feb-2013-team-05.title: Entries are determined by the first row and column
hmmt-feb-2013-team-05.body:
Work modulo $2013$. Suppose row $i$ is used $r_i$ times (subtracting) and column $j$ is used $c_j$ times (adding). The result is $a_{ij}-r_i+c_j\equiv0$, i.e. $a_{ij}\equiv r_i-c_j$ for all $i,j$.

*Necessary:* then $a_{i1}+a_{1j}-a_{11}\equiv(r_i-c_1)+(r_1-c_j)-(r_1-c_1)=r_i-c_j\equiv a_{ij}$. So every entry is determined by the first row and first column.

*Sufficient:* if $a_{ij}\equiv a_{i1}+a_{1j}-a_{11}$ for all $i,j$, take $r_i=a_{i1}$ and $c_j=a_{11}-a_{1j}$; then $r_i-c_j\equiv a_{ij}$ and all entries become $0$ mod $2013$.

An entry between $1$ and $2013$ is a unique representative of its residue, so the good arrays correspond to free choices of the $2013+2012=4025$ entries in the first row and column: $2013^{4025}$ arrays.

**Answer: $2013^{4025}$**

hmmt-feb-2013-team-06.title: Ptolemy
hmmt-feb-2013-team-06.body:
Since $AD$ bisects $\angle A$, $D$ is the midpoint of arc $BC$, so $DB=DC$. By the incenter-excenter lemma, $DB=DC=DI$.

Ptolemy on cyclic quadrilateral $ABDC$: $AB\cdot DC+AC\cdot DB=AD\cdot BC$. With $DB=DC$: $DB\,(AB+AC)=AD\cdot BC$. Since $AB+AC=2BC$: $2DB\cdot BC=AD\cdot BC$, so $AD=2DB=2DI$. Hence $I$ lies on segment $AD$ with $DI=\frac12AD$, i.e. $I$ is the midpoint. ∎

hmmt-feb-2013-team-06.title: Homothety
hmmt-feb-2013-team-06.body: Let $P,Q$ be the midpoints of $AB,AC$ and $E$ the point of $BC$ with $BE=BP=\frac{AB}2$. Then $CE=BC-BE=\frac{AB+AC}2-\frac{AB}2=\frac{AC}2=CQ$, so $BPE$ and $CQE$ are isosceles; also $\frac{BE}{EC}=\frac{AB}{AC}$, so by the angle bisector theorem $E$ lies on the bisector of $\angle A$. The bisector of $\angle B$ is the perpendicular bisector of $PE$ (apex angle bisector of the isosceles triangle) and likewise for $C$ and $QE$, so $I$ is the circumcenter of $PQE$, hence lies on the perpendicular bisector of $PQ$. The perpendicular bisector of $BC$ meets $AI$ at $D$. The homothety at $A$ with ratio $\frac12$ maps $B,C$ to $P,Q$, hence the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ to that of $PQ$, hence $D\mapsto I$. So $AI=\frac12AD$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2013-team-07.title: Cycle argument
hmmt-feb-2013-team-07.body:
Suppose a distribution $D$ gives child $C_i$ the toy $T_i$, and no child gets their favorite toy. Let $T'_i\ne T_i$ be the favorite toy of $C_i$, and note that $T'_i$ is held by some child, say $C_{f(i)}\neq C_i$. Start with $C_{i_1}$ and let $i_{k+1}=f(i_k)$. Since there are finitely many children, the sequence eventually repeats; take a cycle $C_{j_1}\to C_{j_2}\to\cdots\to C_{j_r}\to C_{j_1}$ ($r\ge2$) in which each child's favorite toy is currently held by the next.

Now pass toys around this cycle so that each child $C_{j_s}$ receives the toy currently held by $C_{j_{s+1}}$, their favorite. Everyone outside the cycle keeps their toy. In the new distribution every child on the cycle gets a strictly better toy (their favorite, which is not their old toy) and everyone else is unchanged. So it dominates $D$. Hence $D$ was dominated.

The contrapositive: a distribution that is not dominated must give at least one child their favorite toy. ∎

hmmt-feb-2013-team-08.title: Homotheties
hmmt-feb-2013-team-08.body:
Let $H=CA\cap\omega$ (second point) and $G=BH\cap\omega_B$. The homothety at $A$ taking $\omega_A\to\omega$ sends $F\mapsto E$ and $C\mapsto H$; the homothety at $B$ taking $\omega_B\to\omega$ sends $C\mapsto E$ and $G\mapsto H$. Hence $CF\parallel EH\parallel CG$, so $C,F,G$ are collinear on a line perpendicular to $CD$.

Because $\angle FCD=\angle GCD=90^\circ$, $DF$ and $DG$ are diameters of $\omega_A$ and $\omega_B$. The ratio of the radii of $\omega_A,\omega_B$ is, via the two homotheties, $\frac{CF}{EH}\cdot\frac{EH}{CG}=\frac{CF}{CG}$. Also $\frac{DF}{DG}=\frac{r_A}{r_B}=\frac{CF}{CG}$. So the right triangles $DCF$ and $DCG$ share the leg $DC$ and have hypotenuse and other leg in the same ratio; this forces $DF=DG$, i.e. $\omega_A$ and $\omega_B$ have equal radii.

Then $O$ is at equal distance $R-r$ from the centers of $\omega_A$ and $\omega_B$ (internal tangency: $OO_A=OA-O_AA=R-r$), and the radii are equal, so the power of $O$ with respect to both circles is equal: $O$ lies on the radical axis of $\omega_A$ and $\omega_B$, which is line $CD$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2013-team-09.title: Reformulate; part (a) via CRT
hmmt-feb-2013-team-09.body:
Since $xy\equiv1$, $x$ is a unit and $y=x^{-1}$. So $S_m$ is the set of residues mod $m$ of the form $x+x^{-1}$ with $x\in(\mathbb Z/m)^\times$.

(a) Let $a=x+x^{-1}\in S_m$ and $b=y+y^{-1}\in S_n$. By CRT there is a unit $z$ mod $mn$ with $z\equiv x\pmod m$, $z\equiv y\pmod n$, and then $z+z^{-1}\equiv a\pmod m$, $\equiv b\pmod n$. So each pair $(a,b)$ lifts to an element of $S_{mn}$ (by CRT the residue is determined by $(a,b)$), giving $f(mn)\ge f(m)f(n)$. Conversely any $z+z^{-1}\in S_{mn}$ reduces mod $m$ and $n$ to elements of $S_m$, $S_n$, and its class is determined by the pair, so $f(mn)\le f(m)f(n)$. Hence $f(mn)=f(m)f(n)$. ∎

hmmt-feb-2013-team-09.title: Part (b): count classes of $x$
hmmt-feb-2013-team-09.body:
Fix $p^k$. For a unit $x$ let $q(x)=\max\{i\le k:p^i\mid x^2-1\}$, and let $g(x)$ be the number of units $y$ with $y+y^{-1}\equiv x+x^{-1}$, i.e. $(x-y)(xy-1)\equiv0\pmod{p^k}$. Then $f(p^k)=\sum_x\frac1{g(x)}$.

*Case $q(x)\ge k/2$.* Then $p^{\lceil k/2\rceil}\mid(x-1)(x+1)$, and as $p$ is odd, $x\equiv\pm1\pmod{p^{\lceil k/2\rceil}}$, so $(x\mp1)^2\equiv0\pmod{p^k}$ and $x+x^{-1}\equiv\pm2$. Conversely $x+x^{-1}\equiv\pm2$ forces $q(x)\ge k/2$. These $x$ give exactly the $2$ residues $\pm2$ (distinct as $p$ is odd).

*Case $q(x)=i<k/2$.* If $p^j\|x-y$ and $p^{j'}\|xy-1$, then $\min(j,j')\le q(x)$ (from $x^2-1\equiv xy-1$ or $\equiv x(x-y)$), hence $\max(j,j')\ge k-q(x)$. So $y\equiv x$ or $y\equiv x^{-1}\pmod{p^{k-i}}$ (two distinct classes mod $p^{k-i}$ since $p^{i+1}\nmid x^2-1$, and each such $y$ works), so $g(x)=2p^{i}$. The number of units with $q(x)=i$ is $\#\{p^i\mid x^2-1\}-\#\{p^{i+1}\mid x^2-1\}$, which is $p^{k-1}(p-1)-2p^{k-1}=p^{k-1}(p-3)$ for $i=0$ and $2p^{k-i}-2p^{k-i-1}$ for $i\ge1$ (as $x\equiv\pm1\bmod p^i$).

Summing over classes: $f(p^k)=2+\frac{p^{k-1}(p-3)}2+\sum_{i=1}^{\lceil k/2\rceil-1}\frac{2p^{k-i}-2p^{k-i-1}}{2p^i}$. The geometric sum evaluates to $\frac{p^{k-1}-p^{(1+(-1)^k)/2}}{p+1}$, giving the stated closed form.

**Answer (b): $f(p^k)=2+\frac{p^{k-1}(p-3)}2+\frac{p^{k-1}-p^{\frac{1+(-1)^k}2}}{p+1}$**

hmmt-feb-2013-team-10.title: A piece that can slide right
hmmt-feb-2013-team-10.body:
It suffices to show that, for any $D$, the pieces can be slid so that all pairwise distances exceed $D$: with $D$ larger than the diameter of the table, at most one piece remains on the table, and it can then be slid off.

**Claim.** Some piece can be slid arbitrarily far in the positive $x$-direction. For each piece $P_i$ let $B_i$ be a lowest point of its boundary. Call a point *exposed* if the ray from it in the $+x$ direction meets the interior of no piece. The lowest of all the $B_i$ is exposed, so exposed $B_i$ exist. Choose an exposed $B_k$ with maximal $y$-coordinate, and among those one with maximal $x$-coordinate.

Suppose $P_k$ cannot slide to the right. Then the region $R$ swept by $P_k$ (bounded by the right boundary of $P_k$ and the rightward rays from its highest and lowest points) contains interior points of some pieces $P_j$. Because the ray from $B_k$ meets no interior, each blocking piece lies above that ray, so its lowest point $B_j$ lies in $R$ at height at least $y(B_k)$, and by the choice of $B_k$ (maximal height, then maximal $x$) it is strictly higher than $B_k$. Among the blocking pieces take the one with the lowest $B_j$. Then $B_j$ is exposed (anything to its right in the swept strip would also block $P_k$ and have a lower lowest point, or lie beyond $R$ and hence not meet the ray), and it is higher than $B_k$, contradicting the choice of $B_k$. Hence $P_k$ slides freely to the right.

**Finishing.** Remove this piece (slide it $nD$ to the right), then apply the claim to the remaining pieces and slide the next one $(n-1)D$ to the right, and so on. In finitely many steps all pieces are at pairwise distance at least $D$ (even after projecting to the $x$-axis). ∎
